Metallaphotoredox-catalyzed C–H activation:
regio-selective annulation of allenes with
benzamide†‡
Tianlei Li,
 §a,b Jishun Li,§a,b,c Zihao Zhu,a Yuyuan Chen,a Xueyao Li,a
Qingyun Yang,a Jie Xia,a Wenxuan Zhang,
 a Chao Zhang,*d Weidong Pan*b,c and
Song Wu*a
We have developed an e ﬃcient annulation of benzamides with allenes using cobalt and photoredox dual
catalysis under an oxygen atmosphere. This reaction provides a mild and environmentally friendly method
for the construction of isoquinolinone sca ﬀolds in good to excellent yields, demonstrating broad sub-
strate scopes, high regioselectivity, and good functional group compatibility. Notably, the transformation
features an alternative strategy for the regeneration of a cobalt catalyst with the aid of Eosin Y. Preliminary
mechanistic studies reveal that a radical-mediated cascade annulation is involved in this reaction.
Introduction
Transition-metal-catalyzed direct C –H functionalizations have
emerged as e ﬃcient, powerful, and straightforward approaches
for the construction of carbon –carbon and carbon –heteroatom
bonds over the past few decades. 1 Recently, low-cost and earth-
abundant first-row transition metals came to prominence as
an appealing alternative to noble metals. 2 Among the first-row
transition metals, the unique properties of cobalt in varied oxi-
dation states have witnessed the powerful ability to manipulate
various chemical bonds as a result of the chelation-assisted
direct metalation.
3 Among such elegant transformations, a
number of C –H activation and oxidative annulation reactions
with various unsaturated coupling partners, such as alkynes
and alkenes, have garnered considerable attention for building
molecule diversity via step- and atom-economical strategies.
4
Allenes, bearing two orthogonal cumulative carbon –carbon
double bonds, have been applied to a wide variety of annula-
tions.5 Various noble second- and third-row transition metals
such as Pd, 6 Ir,7 Rh,8 and Ru, 9 have been employed for the
preparation of cyclic sca ﬀolds from simple, nonfunctionalized
acyclic starting materials. Moreover, the first-row transition
metals, such as Mn,
10 Fe,11 Ni,12 and Co,13,14 have been recog-
nized as cheap, environmentally friendly and e ﬀective catalysts
for C –H functionalization with allenes. Particularly, cobalt-
catalyzed regioselective intermolecular cyclization reactions of
arylamides or alkenylamides with allenes were independently
reported by the group of Volla, 14a Rao,14c Cheng,14e Zhai,14g
and Ackermann, 15 which provided rapid synthetic routes for
diverse isoquinoline sca ﬀolds. Notably, di ﬀerent reactivity pat-
terns for the annulation could be observed in Volla ’s work
through tuning electronic properties of the allenes, which led
to e ﬃcient and rapid construction of dihydroisoquinolin-1
(2H)-ones, isoquinolin-1(2 H)-ones, etc. (Scheme 1a). Generally,
stoichiometric amounts of metal oxidants (Ag 2CO3, Mn(OAc) 2,
Mn(OAc)3, etc.), which could re-oxidize a low valent cobalt and
complete the reaction cycle, were commonly employed in these
reported cobalt-catalyzed annulation reactions of arylamides
with allenes (Scheme 1a).
13,14 Recently, the Ackermann group
disclosed an electrochemical C –H activation with allenes
which enabled the high valent cobalt regeneration by anodic
oxidation (Scheme 1a). 15
In recent years, significant progress has been achieved
based on visible light-mediated photoredox catalysis, 16 which
emerged as a sustainable and versatile platform for the devel-
opment of practical synthetic methodologies. Among these,
the merge of transition metal catalysis and photocatalysis,

termed metallaphotoredox catalysis, a ﬀords a distinct reaction
environment, with both oxidation and reduction of organic
and organometallic species simultaneously possible.
17 On the
basis of the huge advantage of metallaphotoredox catalysis in
organic synthesis, we imagined that the development of
cobalt-catalyzed C –H annulation of allenes with benzamide
could be an important complement to the reported strategies.
Previous cyclic voltammetry study revealed Co(OAc)
2 to have
a high oxidation potential, which meant the cobalt( III) could
not be easily generated from Co( II) with common photocata-
lysts. However, the in situ generated cobalt catalyst between
Co(OAc)2 and benzamide substrate showed a lower oxidation
potential at 1.19 V vs. SCE,18 indicating an accessible photo-
redox mediated cobalt( II/III) single-electron oxidation
(Scheme 1b). 19 Thus, we sought to regenerate the cobalt cata-
lyst through a single electron transfer (SET) process assisted by
a photocatalyst under the irradiation of light, which might
avoid the use of metal oxidants (Scheme 1b). Herein, we report
the application of a cobalt and photoredox dual catalysis strat-
egy to the annulation of benzamides with allenes, which pro-
vides an economic and atom-e ﬃcient approach for the syn-
thesis of isoquinolinones (Scheme 1c).
Results and discussion
As illustrated in Table 1, benzamides 1a and benzyl buta-2,3-
dienoate (2a) were exploited as model substrates with 10 mol%
Co(acac)2, 0.2 equiv. of NaOPiv and 5.0 mol% photoredox cata-
lyst under visible light irradiation (15 W CFL) for 24 h at room
temperature under an oxygen atmosphere. The model reaction
was preferentially performed using 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (TFE)
as a solvent, mainly because of its ability to pair with hydro-
gen-bond acceptor groups and interfere positively with the
catalytic cycle.
20 To our delight, the desired product 3a could
be obtained when [Ru(bpy) 3]2+Cl2 was used as a photoredox
catalyst (entry 1). It was found that [Ir(dF(CF 3)ppy)2(dtbbpy)]
PF6 did not e ﬀectively promote this cyclization (entry 2).

reactions with allenes.

Compared with [Ru(bpy) 3]2+Cl2, Eosin Y slightly increased the
annulation yields under the similar reaction conditions
(entry 3). Further experiment revealed that the use of KOTf as a
base could accelerate the reaction and e ﬀectively improve the
yield of 3a (entries 4 and 5). Interestingly, a slight increase in
the amount of cobalt had a significant e ﬀect in promoting the
reaction, and the excellent yield was obtained when the annu-
lation reaction was performed with 20 mol% Co(acac)
2 under
the similar reaction conditions (entry 6). In addition, control
experiments indicated that in the absence of photocatalyst,
Co(acac)
2 or oxygen, the reaction was strongly inhibited
(entries 7 –10). It is worthy to note that light played a crucial
role for the annulation reaction, which stopped at 14% yield
when the reaction was performed in dark (entry 11). When
benzamides with a weaker directing group were employed
instead of 1a, the desired product was not obtained under
standard conditions. In these cases, the starting materials
were fully recovered or decomposed.
With the optimized conditions in hand, the annulation
reaction scope was investigated using various substituted ben-
zamides and allenes, and the results were presented in
Scheme 2. We found that a number of arylamides bearing
diﬀerent substitutions at the ortho-, meta-, and para-positions
were compatible with the optimized conditions (Scheme 2,
3a–3p). For para-substituents in the carboxamides, such as
halogen ( 3f–3h), acetyl ( 3i), cyano ( 3j), or electron-donating
methyl ( 3k), cyclohexyl ( 3l), methoxyl ( 3m) groups, the desired
isoquinolinones were produced in excellent yields. It was
found that the reaction of meta-substituted benzamide furn-
ished two expected regioisomers in good yields ( 3n). On the
other hand, the substrates incorporated with electron-with-
drawing ortho-substituents, such as halogen ( 3b–3c) and tri-
fluoromethyl (3d) groups, were e ﬃciently transformed into the
corresponding products in excellent yields. With an ortho-
methoxy substrate ( 3e), the cyclization process took a short
reaction time, but a slightly reduced product yield was
observed. In the case of disubstituted benzamide ( 3o), the
reaction also gave the desired product in good yield.
Additionally, the naphthoamide ( 3p) was smoothly converted
into the three ring-fused heterocycle in good yield.
Next, the scope of allenes was investigated extensively. As
summarized in Scheme 3, various allenes reacted smoothly
with benzamides under the optimized conditions to produce
the corresponding isoquinolinones in good to excellent yields.
Notably, it was found that the cyclization reaction featured
excellent chemo- and regioselectivity, and solely occurred at
the terminal position of allenes. Various electronically
diverged allenes ( 2b–2f )w e r ee ﬃciently converted into the
desired products ( 4a–4p). A heteroaromatic substrate also
showed good reactivity, and thieno[3,2- c]pyridin-4(5H)-one
derivative ( 4h) was e ﬃciently obtained in good yield.
Gratifyingly, excellent yields ( 4i–4n) were obtained when diphe-
nyl( propa-1,2-dien-1-yl)phosphine oxide ( 2e) was used. In the
case of ethyl penta-3,4-dienoate ( 2f ), the desired isoquinoli-
nones ( 4o and 4p)w e r ea ﬀorded as single regioisomers with
moderate yields. Interestingly, when a terminal disubstituted
allene ( 2g) was used as a coupling partner, the reaction only
aﬀorded the corresponding exo-cyclic isoquinolinones ( 4q–4s)
in moderate to good yields. These results provide useful infor-
mation for the mechanistic perspective on the migratory allene
insertion/isomerization manifold.
Generally, the formation of either alkenyl-metal or metal-
π-allyl intermediates is dependent on the nature of allenes and
metals in the transition-metal-catalyzed C –H

functionalization.5,14,15 Volla and co-workers first disclosed
that the regioselectivity of this annulation is dominated by the
coordinative insertion of the double bond of an allene in
cobalt-catalyzed reactions and that the electronical properties
of allenes have a great influence on the reactivity of annula-
tion.
14a To our delight, the same results were obtained in our
system. The carbocobaltation of phenylallene occurred at the
more electron-rich double bond via formation of a stable Co- σ-
allyl complex. 14a Various isoquinolinones with an exo-double
bond were obtained by coupling benzamides with propa-1,2-
dien-1-ylbenzene ( 2i) under the standard conditions
(Scheme 4). A number of ary amides ( 5a–5d) and heterocyclic
derivatives, such as thiophene ( 5e), showed good compatibility
with the reaction condition. Moreover, we investigated substi-
tuted phenylallenes such as 2j, 2k and 2l with di ﬀerent benz-
amide, and the reaction provided the desired products in mod-
erate yields.
A gram-scale reaction was conducted to assess the
eﬃciency of this protocol (Scheme 5). Two isoquinolinones
were furnished by employing 20 mol% Co(acac) 2 and
2.0 equiv. of preformed allene 2e in 79% and 87% yield,
respectively (for details, please see ESI ‡). The structure and
regioselectivity of the nitro substituted isoquinolinone ( 4n)
were confirmed unambiguously by the X-ray crystallography.
As shown in the post-annulation Wittig reaction, the cycliza-
tion product ( 4m) was e ﬃciently transformed into olefin 6
with good yield.
To gain further mechanistic insights, a series of control
experiments were carried out. A mixture of benzamides
[D5]-1a/1a (1 : 1) was used to react with allenylphsphine oxide
2e under optimized conditions, and the KIE experiments gave
a k
H/kD value of 1.1. This result indicated that C –H bond acti-
vation might not be involved in the rate-determining step
(Scheme 6a). Furthermore, no H/D exchange was observed
when [D5]- 1a was treated with phosphinoylallene under stan-
dard conditions. Similarly, no deuterium incorporation in the
product 4n was observed when 1c was treated with isotopically
labelled CD
3OD as a cosolvent. These results suggested that
the C –H cobaltation step should be irreversible (Scheme 6a). A
control reaction performed with stoichiometric TEMPO
(2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-1-piperidinyloxy, a common radical sca-

venger) formed no desired product under the standard con-
dition (Scheme 6b). This gave a clue that a highly reactive
radical species might be involved in the catalytic cycle.
Additionally, the cyclization reaction conducted under an
oxygen atmosphere in the absence of Eosin Y did not generate
the desired product. It excluded the possibility of oxygen
acting as a single oxidant that regenerated the cobalt catalyst.
On the other hand, the result of the intermolecular compe-
tition experiment showed that the electron-rich amide 1e was
favorable over 1d only slightly, suggesting little electronic influ-
ence in the C –H metalation (Scheme 6c).
Furthermore, detailed cyclic voltammetry studies were
carried out to gain a better understanding of this annulation
reaction. As shown in Scheme 7, the oxidation potential of sub-
strate 1a was 1.52 V vs. SCE, and 2a had no relevant oxidation
potential. The in situ generated cobalt catalyst
18 revealed a
lower oxidation potential at 0.94 V vs. SCE, which might be oxi-
dized by the photoexcited Eosin Y* (0.83 V vs. SCE).21 These
results demonstrated that a Co( II/III) single electron oxidation
might occur in the initial step of this reaction.
Based on the mechanistic experiments described above, a
plausible mechanism for this reaction was proposed in
Scheme 8. The first step begins with the ligand exchange to
generate the cobalt( II)-benzamide from Co(acac) 2, followed by
oxidation of Co( II)t oC o ( III) occurring simultaneously with
reduction of Eosin Y*. Additional ligand exchange and coordi-
nation with 1a furnishes Co(
III)-intermediate A. Interestingly,
this intermediate was observed by subjecting stoichiometric
Co(acac)2 to the standard conditions (for details, see ESI ‡).22
Subsequently, activation of the inert aryl C –H bond forms the
key metallacycle Co( III) intermediate B, which gives C upon
allene coordination. Regioselective insertion of the C –Co bond
into a π-bond of the allene gives the seven membered cobalta-
cycle intermediate D or E. The selectivity of the migratory
insertion depends on the steric and electronic characteristics
of the substituted allenes. When allenes were substituted by
an electronic-withdrawing group (R in C), the insertion took
place in the less-substituted double bond, leading to inter-
mediate D. When R was a phenyl group, the addition was apt
to occur at a more substituted double bond, furnishing inter-
mediate E with high selectivity. The C –N bond-forming reduc-
tive elimination gives the cyclic product (isoquinolidinone I or
G) and the cobalt(
I) intermediate F. Intermediate F formed as
a result of the reductive elimination then undergoes coordi-
nation with 1a and might be oxidized by the photoexcited
Eosin Y* (0.83 V vs. SCE)
21 (the incipient cobalt catalyst from
Co(acac)2 and benzamide 1a showed an oxidation potential of
0.94 V vs. SCE). Thus, a Co( III) species could be regenerated
with simultaneous formation of a reductive Eosin Y radical
anion ( −1.06 V vs. SCE).21 The Eosin Y radical anion might be
oxidized to the ground state by O 2 to complete the photoredox
cycle.21 At last, the isoquinolidinone intermediate G formed

Conclusions
In conclusion, we have developed an e ﬃcient protocol for the
construction of isoquinoline sca ﬀolds ones by merging cobalt
(III)-catalyzed C–H functionalization with visible light mediated
photoredox catalysis. Notably, no metal oxidants are required
in this transformation. The reaction provides a mild and envir-
onmentally friendly route for the e ﬃcient synthesis of isoqui-
nolinones and isoquinolidinones. A wide substrate scope, high
level of chemoselectivity and regioselectivity, and broad func-
tional group tolerance were observed. Preliminary mechanistic
studies reveal that a radical-mediated cascade annulation is
involved in this reaction. Further studies about synthetic appli-
cations and reaction mechanism are currently ongoing in our
laboratory.
Author contributions
Tianlei Li, Jishun Li, Zihao Zhu, Yuyuan Chen, Xueyao Li, and
Wenxuan Zhang conducted the experiments and prepared the
ESI.‡ Tianlei Li, Jie Xia and Qingyun Yang characterized and
analyzed the X-ray crystal data. Tianlei Li, Song Wu, Weidong
Pan and Chao Zhang designed the experiments and wrote the
paper. All authors have given approval to the final version of
the manuscript.
